One of the lectionary readings for the middle of this season is John 2:13- 23, an account of Jesus cleansing the Temple in Jerusalem. Unfortunately, much preaching and teaching about this text focuses solely on the reasons for Jesus’ forceful critique of the temple practices of his time without bringing that critique into our time. articles.text: Editor: As PUSD continues to troubleshoot the budget shortfall, a parcel tax increase is one of the scenarios worth exploring. While any tax increase should rightfully be met with scrutiny, this tax is a logical investment in our homes. I live on the border of Piedmont. The homes on our side of the street are in Piedmont and the homes on the other side - just 30 feet away - are in Oakland. A simple Redfin or Zillow search shows that the pricing for the homes on our side are valued an average of 41% higher than the homes on the Oakland side of the street. Like many families who live in Piedmont, we moved here for the great community, and the usual reasons of good weather and proximity to jobs. All good reasons, but not good enough to explain why we would pay 40%+ more for our home when we could live 30 feet away and still meet those same criteria. For us and many Piedmonters, we moved to Piedmont for its schools. When looking at comparable neighborhoods, the main cause of significant swings in home pricing is always the quality of the public schools. PUSD provides high-quality public education to our children and enviable student-to-teacher ratios compared with immediately adjacent communities. Everyone is aware of the Piedmont school budget crises, and one of the solutions being discussed is to raise our property taxes to help cover the shortfall. This is not just a tax, it is an investment in the single asset that, for most households, is their largest – their home. The math is very simple. There are est. 4,000 homes in Piedmont. PUSD needs to cover a $2.3 million budget shortfall. If we were to simply increase property taxes to cover this, it would work out to $575 per house per year. Currently all homeowners pay $2,932 per year through Measure G, and $0.25/ft. (on their home square footage) through Measure H. This means an average 2,500 square foot home in Piedmont pays $3,557/year in taxes to support our schools. Add in the $575 increase and this would become $4,132/year. Run that math out 30 years with the mandatory annual increases and these taxes would total approximately $155,000 over 30 years, or $62/ft. on the average 2,500 square foot home. The average home price in Oakland is $608/ft. and in Piedmont it is $946/ft., so for an investment in our schools of $62/ft. you get a return of $338/ft., or about 540% on your money. On an annualized basis over 30 years, this is 11% per year, and if you live in your home less than 30 years the returns are even higher! To put that in context: 30-year U.S. treasuries are yielding around 4.5% per year, so an investment in our schools that helps your community, your neighbors, our teachers and students, would actually give you a return that is almost three times higher. This is what you call a “no-brainer” investment.
articles.title: Investing in our schools is a “no-brainer” investment in our homes

For us and many Piedmonters, we moved to Piedmont for its schools. When looking at comparable neighborhoods, the main cause of significant swings in home pricing is always the quality of the public schools. PUSD provides high-quality public education to our children and enviable student-to-teacher ratios compared with immediately adjacent communities. Everyone is aware of the Piedmont school budget crises, and one of the solutions being discussed is to raise our property taxes to help cover the shortfall. This is not just a tax, it is an investment in the single asset that, for most households, is their largest – their home. The math is very simple. There are est. 4,000 homes in Piedmont. PUSD needs to cover a $2.3 million budget shortfall. If we were to simply increase property taxes to cover this, it would work out to $575 per house per year. Currently all homeowners pay $2,932 per year through Measure G, and $0.25/ft. (on their home square footage) through Measure H. This means an average 2,500 square foot home in Piedmont pays $3,557/year in taxes to support our schools. Add in the $575 increase and this would become $4,132/year. Run that math out 30 years with the mandatory annual increases and these taxes would total approximately $155,000 over 30 years, or $62/ft. on the average 2,500 square foot home. The average home price in Oakland is $608/ft. and in Piedmont it is $946/ft., so for an investment in our schools of $62/ft. you get a return of $338/ft., or about 540% on your money. On an annualized basis over 30 years, this is 11% per year, and if you live in your home less than 30 years the returns are even higher! To put that in context: 30-year U.S. treasuries are yielding around 4.5% per year, so an investment in our schools that helps your community, your neighbors, our teachers and students, would actually give you a return that is almost three times higher. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department’s newest officer, Ashley Gallion, grew up in a tight-knit community where neighbors knew one another and kids played outdoors until nighttime. It was the kind of neighborhood that doesn’t exist in many places. When she first saw Piedmont, she knew she had found something special. “When I came for my first ride-along to see the department, I remember driving in and seeing the kids walking to school. Just seeing them feel safe enough to walk to school. It is exactly like what I had growing up in Morgan Hill, and it was what I always looked for once I left that community.” On January 12, the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) announced that Gallion completed her field training program, making her a fully sworn officer on the police force. She was born in 1996 in Gilroy, and grew up in Morgan Hill, where she lived, and San Jose, where she went to school. She graduated from Branham High School in 2014 and began attending San Jose State the same year, with a major in Psychology. However, she quickly learned that though she liked helping people, she didn’t necessarily like sitting behind a desk all day. She decided to go into law enforcement after a conversation with her grandmother about hostage negotiations. “My grandma had read something in a newspaper about hostage negotiating, and she brought it up to me. ‘You know, this is all the things you like intertwined into one. You get to use your psychology degree, but you get to help people, be outside, and really feel like you’re making a difference.” Photo by April Fitzgerald Officer Ashley completed her field training program on January 12 and is now a fully sworn officer with Piedmont Police Department. This was the turning point in her career. “It switched on something for me. That’s when I knew I wanted to go into law enforcement,” she said. In 2018, Gallion left SJSU to become a Community Service Officer with the San Jose Police Department. There she met Jessica Morey, now also a member of the PPD, and the two became close friends. Morey found her way to Piedmont through a mutual friend who put her in contact with Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. A ride-along was organized where Gallion and Morey could see the city, and she was impressed. “When Jessica and I left the city, we were both in such awe. We looked at each other and said this is where we belong.’” These days, Gallion doesn’t think about a job in hostage negotiation as much, but she still identifies with the sentiment of helping others in need. Overall, she hopes she can serve the Piedmont community well in her role. “I am here and ready whenever they need me, and I’m fortunate I have the opportunity to be a person they can count on,” she said.

articles.text: Nicole Virgil, practitioner of Christian Science healing and public speaker, will present a talk, “Be set free,” on Sunday, March 24, at 2:00 p.m. at First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland, located at 1880 Mountain Blvd. in the Montclair district. The talk will focus on universal healing precepts found in the Holy Bible, especially in Christ Jesus’ life and teachings, showing how they are available for anyone to understand and experience through the lens of Christian Science. The talk is free, open to the community, and sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland. “Circumstances often present what appear to be significant obstacles to living freely, something that everyone wants to do,” Ms. Virgil says. “In this talk, we will examine liberty from a Biblical perspective; and see how real people today find their freedom from all kinds of physical, emotional and circumstantial restrictions that seem clearly beyond their control.” Sharing examples of healing from her own life and professional practice of Christian Science, Ms. Virgil will explain why Christian Science is both Christian and scientific, meaning that people can prove its effectiveness for themselves, as fully described in the book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, written by the founder of the Christian Science movement, Mary Baker Eddy. Ms. Virgil will also touch on the life of Mary Baker Eddy, who came to understand, confirm, and teach what she felt was original Christian healing. Eddy herself said she was especially inspired by Jesus’ demand, “He that believes on me, the works that I do will he do also; and greater works than these will he do, because I go unto my Father” (found in the Gospel of John 14:12 in the Bible). For over 150 years, people around the world have worked to follow Christ Jesus in this practice of Christianity and continue to do so today, experiencing healings of physical ills and personal difficulties. articles.text: Lateefah Simon, a member of the BART board of directors, has emerged as the apparent frontrunner in the race for the 12th Congressional District, which has been held by Rep. Barbara Lee (D) since 1998. Lee is currently a candidate for the Senate seat of the late Dianne Feinstein. Simon, based in Emeryville, has raised more than $1.1 million according to the Federal Elections Commission and has received endorsements from Governor Gavin Newsom, Barbara Lee, and the California Democratic Party. In addition to her broad appeal, Simon has also shown interest in Piedmont in recent statements, including a willingness to taking over Lee’s speaking role at the annual Martin Luther King Jr. celebration in Piedmont if elected. “If I have the honor of being elected to Congress, I’ll be a voice for all residents of the 12th Congressional district, including Piedmont,” said Ms. Simon. “With my background as an Lateefah Simon organizer and community leader, I understand the importance of staying connected to the communities I serve. One of my top priorities will be to build a strong district office with accessible and responsive staff to provide constituent services.” Simon acknowledged that she would have big shoes to fill if elected to Lee’s seat in Congress. “It would be the honor of my life to continue the legacy of Congresswoman Barbara Lee by representing the East Bay in Washington. Congresswoman Lee has championed our East Bay values and stood up for peace and justice on the national stage [...] I plan on being a fighter for this community.” On January 31, Lee officially endorsed Simon. “After his 27 years of service, [Ron Dellums] passed the baton to me, and now I am excited and proud to endorse Lateefah Simon, my former student, to run this next lap of the race,” said Lee. When asked if she would take over Barbara Lee’s longtime speaker role at Piedmont’s annual MLK Jr. celebration if elected, Ms. Simon was enthusiastic. “Absolutely! I’d be honored to join the people of Piedmont in celebrating Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s legacy. Events like this are what keep the memory of the civil rights movement alive. Count me in.” The 12th Congressional District’s general election will be on November 5, 2024.

articles.text: As most people in Piedmont know, Piedmont’s School board is issuing major budget cuts to the art and dance departments, starting as early as March 15. As a current student I can state that art and dance are both activities that give me great joy and passion. For many, art and dance are escapes or creative outlets. In straining times for adolescents, they are key activities that help to release stress and improve mood. The thought of them possibly being cut from the school curriculum fills many with great sadness and frustration. Art has long been overlooked as nothing more than “pretty paintings” or modernistic statements few can understand. In reality, that is far from the truth. Art can take many forms and shapes, one of them being dance, also deemed unimportant by the school board and set for cuts. The school board has already faced major pushback from the community in response to their recent decision. articles.text: As the world of standardized testing continues to evolve in a “post” pandemic era, many families wonder how AP exams, which take place each May, fit into their student’s college roadmap. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked. • Do AP exams actually matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes. AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must she take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. If the test goes well, they have a great quantitative addition to their apps. • My student is doing well in the AP class. Will he do well on the AP exam? This is a tricky one. AP classes are not standardized like the exam; there is often great variety in rigor, grading, and expectations. The best way to know how a student will do on an AP exam is by taking a practice test. • If my student’s AP class isn’t doing much to prepare her for the exam, what can she do? All students who are enrolled in an AP course have access to “AP classroom”. This is a great resource for official practice problems and course content. If a student wants more individualized support, they can always talk to their teacher or engage a tutor. There are now a total of 39 AP courses (although few schools offer the full range of classes). APs are meant to be an opportunity for students to delve into topics of interest while also challenging themselves with college level coursework. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked. • Do AP exams actually matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes. AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must she take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. If the test goes well, they have a great quantitative addition to their apps. • My student is doing well in the AP class. Will he do well on the AP exam? This is a tricky one. AP classes are not standardized like the exam; there is often great variety in rigor, grading, and expectations. The best way to know how a student will do on an AP exam is by taking a practice test. • If my student’s AP class isn’t doing much to prepare her for the exam, what can she do? All students who are enrolled in an AP course have access to “AP classroom”. This is a great resource for official practice problems and course content. If a student wants more individualized support, they can always talk to their teacher or engage a tutor. There are now a total of 39 AP courses (although few schools offer the full range of classes). APs are meant to be an opportunity for students to delve into topics of interest while also challenging themselves with college level coursework. While AP classes and exams can be an important factor in college admissions, their true intent is to help students gain important knowledge and skills that will help them succeed in college and beyond. articles.text: A couple of weeks ago two troops from the Piedmont Scout Council headed into the mountains for a weekend full of snow, fun, and fellowship. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball season is off to a delayed start after having its opening games rained out on Thursday and Friday, February 29 and March 1. On Tuesday, March 5, the Highlanders season began in earnest, with a 12-2 thumping of Salesian at Humphries Diamond. It was a complete day, with eight hits and drawing eight walks to activate the 10-run rule to end the game after five innings. On the mound, senior John Olsen and George Bishop got the job done with a combined three hits allowed. Olsen got the win with four innings of work including two strikeouts and allowed no earned runs. “We have a lot of guys we’ll put on the mound and we trust them. John was great for us last year and he’ll throw a lot,” said coach Eric Olson, Senior Peter Krumins showed off his power hitting by going a perfect 3-for-3 with a pair of doubles that broke the game open. He finished with four RBIs and three runs scored. Catcher Will Parker, who hits in the three spot, also had a big afternoon, going 3-for-4 with a double and three RBIs. 12-2 over Salesian After a 1-2-3 top of the first by Olsen, PHS got the show started with a single by Markos Lagios, a walk by Krumins, and a single to bring in Lagios. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos then brought in Krumins in a fielder’s choice. Although Salesian scored twice in the top of the third to tie it at 2-2, it was the last time they got on the scoreboard. PHS scored three runs in the bottom half when Krumins slugged a double to left field, followed by Parker hitting a single. After Papahadjopoulos drew a walk, Brandon Dicke brought in Krumins on a ground out. Diego Delventhal then hit a single to right field to score Parker and Papahadjopoulos for a 5-2 score. Olsen then forced another 1-2-3 inning in the top of the fourth, leading to another 3-run inning. It started with Jack Meyjes reaching on an error, then loading the bases with walks to Ellis Moss and Lagios. Krumins hit a two-run single to score Moss and Meyjes. With one out, Papahadjopoulos drew another walk followed by Dicke bringing in Lagios on a fielder’s choice for an 8-2 lead. In the bottom of the fifth, Jordan Vo and Meyjes got things started with a pair of walks, then Lagios drew a walk to load the bases with one out. That’s when Krumins drove a shot to the left field fence for another double, bringing in Vo and Mayjes to score. Parker then stepped to the plate. On the second pitch of his at bat, Parker smacked a double of his own to deep center field, resulting in Lagios and Krumins crossing home to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles, three runs scored, four RBIs, and a Staff Photos Pitcher John Olsen got the start for Piedmont, throwing six strikeouts and allowing no earned runs. walk. Lagios went 1-for-2 with three runs, two walks, and a stolen base. Parker was 3-for-4 with a double, three RBIs, and one run. Papahadjopoulos had an RBI, run scored, and two walks. Dicke had two RBIs. Delventhal was 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Meyjes scored two runs and drew a walk. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) travels to San Leandro tomorrow, March 7, for a 3:30 p.m. game with the Pirates. They will host Justin-Siena in a traditional home opener on Saturday, March 9 at 12:00 p.m. Peter Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles and four RBIs. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got its season started in a big way, winning its first two games in the past week, They defeated Dublin 12-5 on the road Wednesday, February 28, and won handily 14-2 over HeadRoyce for their home opener at Witter Field on Monday, March 4. “It was really good we played that Dublin game. They were a very physical team, and our defense wasn’t really set. The Dublin game was helpful in putting that together. We really came together against Head-Royce,” coach Carlton Chan said. The pair of games was good preparation for some difficult competition. Piedmont plays at Acalanes tonight, March 6. The Dons are currently 3-1 and compete in North Coast Section’s Division 2 alongside Piedmont. Piedmont’s attack featured six different goal scorers against Dublin and different goal scorers against Head-Royce. Hallie Burden made an impact in face-offs, winning seven draws against Head-Royce and three versus Dublin. Ruby Guzdar, a leading scorer from last year, scored five goals against Dublin, and Laurel Bentley had a hat trick in the win over Head-Royce. “I said early on that Hallie was going to be important on the draw and she showed it today. Our plays are starting to come together,” Chan said. 14-2 win vs. Head-Royce PHS led 6-0 by the end of the first quarter and the route was on. It ballooned to 11-0 by halftime. With a running clock for the entire second half, PHS extended the lead to 13-1 through the third quarter and added one more goal in the final going. Piedmont wasted no time. On Tuesday, March 5, the Highlanders season began in earnest, with a 12-2 thumping of Salesian at Humphries Diamond. It was a complete day, with eight hits and drawing eight walks to activate the 10-run rule to end the game after five innings. On the mound, senior John Olsen and George Bishop got the job done with a combined three hits allowed. Olsen got the win with four innings of work including two strikeouts and allowed no earned runs. “We have a lot of guys we’ll put on the mound and we trust them. John was great for us last year and he’ll throw a lot,” said coach Eric Olson, Senior Peter Krumins showed off his power hitting by going a perfect 3-for-3 with a pair of doubles that broke the game open. He finished with four RBIs and three runs scored. Catcher Will Parker, who hits in the three spot, also had a big afternoon, going 3-for-4 with a double and three RBIs. 12-2 over Salesian After a 1-2-3 top of the first by Olsen, PHS got the show started with a single by Markos Lagios, a walk by Krumins, and a single to bring in Lagios. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos then brought in Krumins in a fielder’s choice. Although Salesian scored twice in the top of the third to tie it at 2-2, it was the last time they got on the scoreboard. PHS scored three runs in the bottom half when Krumins slugged a double to left field, followed by Parker hitting a single. After Papahadjopoulos drew a walk, Brandon Dicke brought in Krumins on a ground out. Diego Delventhal then hit a single to right field to score Parker and Papahadjopoulos for a 5-2 score. Olsen then forced another 1-2-3 inning in the top of the fourth, leading to another 3-run inning. It started with Jack Meyjes reaching on an error, then loading the bases with walks to Ellis Moss and Lagios. Krumins hit a two-run single to score Moss and Meyjes. With one out, Papahadjopoulos drew another walk followed by Dicke bringing in Lagios on a fielder’s choice for an 8-2 lead. In the bottom of the fifth, Jordan Vo and Meyjes got things started with a pair of walks, then Lagios drew a walk to load the bases with one out. That’s when Krumins drove a shot to the left field fence for another double, bringing in Vo and Mayjes to score. Parker then stepped to the plate. On the second pitch of his at bat, Parker smacked a double of his own to deep center field, resulting in Lagios and Krumins crossing home to activate the 10-run rule. Lagios went 1-for-2 with three runs, two walks, and a stolen base. Parker was 3-for-4 with a double, three RBIs, and one run. Papahadjopoulos had an RBI, run scored, and two walks. Dicke had two RBIs. Delventhal was 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Meyjes scored two runs and drew a walk. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got its season started in a big way, winning its first two games in the past week, They defeated Dublin 12-5 on the road Wednesday, February 28, and won handily 14-2 over HeadRoyce for their home opener at Witter Field on Monday, March 4. “It was really good we played that Dublin game. They were a very physical team, and our defense wasn’t really set. The Dublin game was helpful in putting that together. We really came together against Head-Royce,” coach Carlton Chan said. The pair of games was good preparation for some difficult competition. Piedmont plays at Acalanes tonight, March 6. The Dons are currently 3-1 and compete in North Coast Section’s Division 2 alongside Piedmont. Piedmont’s attack featured six different goal scorers against Dublin and different goal scorers against Head-Royce. Hallie Burden made an impact in face-offs, winning seven draws against Head-Royce and three versus Dublin. Ruby Guzdar, a leading scorer from last year, scored five goals against Dublin, and Laurel Bentley had a hat trick in the win over Head-Royce. “I said early on that Hallie was going to be important on the draw and she showed it today. Our plays are starting to come together,” Chan said. 14-2 win vs. Head-Royce PHS led 6-0 by the end of the first quarter and the route was on. It ballooned to 11-0 by halftime. With a running clock for the entire second half, PHS extended the lead to 13-1 through the third quarter and added one more goal in the final going. Piedmont wasted no time. Friedie Schickedanz scored a goal on the first possession of the game. Burden then scored two minutes later after drawing a shooting space penalty. Chloe Graham assisted Luisa Cole for a goal, and Graham scored with 4:52 left in the first period. Peyton Watson launched one in after another two minutes, and Guzdar capped off the quarter for a 6-0 advantage. In the second quarter, Watson scored after 33 seconds, while Burden made it 8-0 with 8:37 left in the half—then she scored again after another 45 seconds. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont starts its season with two low-scoring defensive losses. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team showed good defense in its first pair of games of the spring season, but fell 7-3 to Serra in San Mateo on Thursday, February 28 and 6-4 to Casa Grande on Friday, March 1 at Witter Field. Offensively senior Rylan Nelson and freshman Connor Fredericks, the younger brothers of Class of 2023 graduates Jack Nelson and Nate Fredericks, were the sparkplugs. Nelson scored three of Piedmont’s goals, two against Serra. Fredericks also scored three total goals, including two against Casa Grande. On defense, goalie Gus Von Metszch made eight saves against Casa Grande and 15 against Serra. The results were seen as encouraging defensive performances against difficult opponents. Piedmont’s full starting lineup has had limited time practicing together. “There was a fair amount of season overlap, so we had mixed numbers through the first two weeks of practice. We finally had full numbers when the winter season wrapped up,” explained first-year coach Jeff Lamb. Piedmont’s season ramps up next week. It plays Washington in Fremont for the Western Alameda County Conference opener tomorrow, March 7, and will face Div. 1 NCS opponent California at home on Friday. It also will play Div. 2 powerhouse Novato at Witter Field on March 12. 6-4 loss to Casa Grande Piedmont trailed 2-1 by the end of the first quarter and 3-2 by halftime. Casa Grande scored three goals in the third quarter while the Highlanders added one to make it 6-3 entering the fourth. PHS didn’t allow another goal in the remaining minutes, but only got one more on the board. Fredericks scored once in the first quarter at the 9:25 mark, but Casa Grande responded two minutes later and took the lead with 4:47 left in the first. Casa Grande extended the lead with slightly less than 10 minutes left in the second quarter, but Oliver Shafroth won the faceoff and scored a goal on the very next possession, 3-2. Rylan Nelson scored three goals in two games. Gus Von Metszch had eight saves against Casa Grande and 15 against Serra.

articles.text: Museo Italo Americano presents “Riccardo Rossati: Villa Arconati & Imaginary Worlds” at Fort Mason Center For Arts and Culture in San Francisco now through March 31. Italian artist Rossati was born in Rome into a family of painters, and studied under celebrated painters in China, Singapore, Thailand and Paris. Rossati is influenced by the alchemy of pigments, and said at a very young age that he discovered the art of oil painting. He studied the masters of the Italian Renaissance and modern expressionism at the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome. This exhibition features the enchanting Villa Arconati, a grand Baroque style palace nestled near the city of Milan. Rossati’s paintings provide a mesmerizing glimpse into the artist’s distinctive perspective of the ItalRiccardo Rossati ian historical site. Hours of the exhibit are Tuesday through Saturday, 12:00 to 4:00 p.m. and Sunday, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The exhibit will be on view through Sunday, March 31. articles.text: Tickets are now on sale for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Art Bash, the museum’s major annual fundraiser that helps fund the museum’s education, family programs and community engagement events, benefiting over 150,000 people every year. This year’s Art Bash begins at 5 p.m. on Wednesday, April 24 with a cocktail reception and immersive dinner experience designed by iconic filmmaker and installation artist Isaac Julien. Julien’s filmmaking career began with his celebrated 1989 drama-documentary Looking for Langston, an exploration of the poet Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2017 Birthday Honors for services to the arts. Art Bash 2024 will feature photography and large-scale images from the artist’s series Ten Thousand Waves. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse presents Rent, directed by Kimberly Dooley, playing onstage now through March 31. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate its brass musicians with an all-brass concert at Davies Symphony Hall this Sunday, March 10. Trumpet, French horn, trombone, and tuba players will be led by conductor Brad Hogarth to bring the instruments’ big, bold and distinctive sound front and center. Hogarth is the Associate Professor of Conducting at San Francisco State University, and was recently named Associate Conductor of the Monterey Symphony. He is the music director and conductor of the Art Haus Collective and is also an accomplished trumpeter who performs regularly with a number of orchestras, including the Indianapolis Symphony and Louisville Orchestra. As a guest conductor, he has appeared with the Diablo Symphony Orchestra, the ECHO Chamber Orchestra, the San Francisco Wind Ensemble and the Oakland Municipal Band. The evening’s program will highlight concert music for brass, percussion, and timpani. The program includes Presto Barbaro from Symphonic Suite Photo by Kristen-Loken San Francisco Symphony brass musicians from On the Waterfront by Leonard Bernstein, Ottoni by Magnus Lindberg, Quatre Motets sur des thèmes grégoriens by Maurice Duruflé, A Moorside Suite by Gustav Holst, Variations on a Theme by Paganini Witold Lutosławski, and Chicago Skyline by Shulamit Ran. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Ticket s /2023 -24/SF- SY M PHO - NY-BRASS.

articles.text: Oakland Ballet’s Dancing Moons Festival takes place in Oakland and San Francisco this Spring. Oakland Ballet will present its third annual Dancing Moons Festival March 14 through April 6 at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland and ODC Theater in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees held at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants through 1910 and 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. March 14 through 16 performances will take place at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland, and April 5 and 6 performances take place at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. Showtimes vary. To purchase tickets, visit https://oaklandballet.org/ dancing-moons-festival/.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, March 6, 2024 MOVIE FOR KIDS Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home By Chris Honoré The year was 1966 and a Sci Fi series called “Star Trek” debuted on television, promising to “boldly go where no man has gone before.” Now, some 44 years later, improbably, “Star Trek” has morphed into a cultural phenomenon resulting in not only television syndication of the original show, but spin offs, books, comics, video games and, for a time, a themed attraction in Las Vegas that drew thousands of what came to be known as “Trekkies.” In other words, Star Trek evolved from those early days into a worldwide entertainment juggernaut, resonating with generations of fans, and possessing a cult following wherein hard-core Trekkies peruse endless layers of narrative minutiae, characterization and predictive technology. In 1979 the first feature length film was made – “Star Trek: The Motion Picture” – launching what would become a successful franchise, starring the original multiethnic cast from the television series. Names such as Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Captain Kirk (William Shatner), Lt. Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), and “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) are now part of our lexicon, as is the phrase, “beam me up.” In fact, NASA named its prototype space shuttle the Enterprise after the fictional starship. Since the first “Star Trek” was screened, 10 movies have followed – the most recent, “Star Trek,” a prequel — with the The cast of Star Trek reprise their role in the movie Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home. 12th in preproduction, due to be released in June of 2012. Their appeal is indisputable. Of all the “Star Trek” films made to date, perhaps the most accessible is “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home,” receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock” and the first few minutes of “Voyage Home” make a loose connection to “III”, “IV” easily stands alone. The premise is deceptively simple: It’s the late 23rd century and a space probe of unknown origins is approaching earth, sending out a signal that is at first indecipherable. The force field from the probe is shutting down all electrical grids on earth and is, in effect, destroying the planet. The crew of the Enterprise, their starship destroyed, and having hijacked a Klingon vessel in need of repairs, is stranded on the planet Vulcan. Their plan is to return to earth and stand trial for crimes against the Federation. They pick up transmissions not only from the probe, but distress calls from earth. Finally breaking the probe’s code, they determine that it is sending out a series of whale calls, or humpback whale songs. Because whales are extinct in the 23rd century, the crew decides that the only solution is to travel back in time, to the late 20th century, beam up two whales, and return them to their time. And so they travel back in time, to San Francisco, landing the cloaked Klingon ship in Golden Gate Park. The crew then ventures forth, walking the streets of San Francisco in search of two whales and a nuclear energy source to power the ship. Their time in San Francisco is inspired. The juxtaposition of the crew with the locals makes for some interesting moments. An embedded joke is that even though they are all dressed in Starfleet uniforms (with the exception of Spock, who is wearing a white terry cloth robe and an aerobic headband to hide his ears), no one pays them any attention. This is, after all, San Francisco, which is very hip and laid-back. The encounters of the crew with the locals are wonderful, often comedic, and just restrained enough to never slide into parody. There’s also a mild romantic tension (atypical to be sure) between Kirk and a marine biologist, Dr. Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks). The conflict in the film stems from the urgency of the hunt. Earth in the future is in peril; time is of the essence. Unlike other “Trek” films, there are no villains in “Voyage Home” – well, perhaps there are, meaning the whalers who have hunted the humpbacks to extinction, a reality that Spock points out is “illogical.” There is, of course, the probe, needed only as a brief catalyst for sending the crew back in time. The co-author and producer of “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home,” Harve Bennett, will make a guest appearance at Saturday’s screening and take questions at the end of the film. Bennett was born in Chicago in 1930 and has spent most of his life, since graduating from UCLA’s film school, producing television shows for ABC and CBS, as well as feature length films. He co-authored, produced, and made cameo appearances in four of the “Star Trek” films – “The Wrath of Khan”; “The Search for Spock”; “The Voyage Home”; and “The Final Frontier.” Now living in Ashland, he considers himself “semi-retired.” Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home. articles.text: Toda,y I found a hang tag on my door from the Piedmont Police informing me that PPD was moving ahead with the next phase of ALPR (Automated License Plate Recognition). This is a very good step. Chief Bowers has said in the past that the ALPRs play an extremely important role in combatting crime in the city. It also reminded me that I had been meaning to address this issue in the Post for many months, but I had not achieved a great enough level of crabbiness to do so. And even though Wiley is feeling pretty mellow today, he’s going to write the article anyway. My shrewd power of observation has led me to deduce that there are a lot of cars in Piedmont without front license plates. In fact, every time I have conducted an informal visual survey at the corner of Oakland and Highland, I have found that about half of the cars that go by have no front plates. My power of analytical thinking has led me to deduce that if a car has both front and back plates, it is significantly more likely to be recognized by the ALPR. And being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Let me repeat that: Being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Who are these scofflaws (what a great word)? Most of them are otherwise law-abiding citizens of Piedmont, who generally stop at stop signs, support our great police department, and keep voting to tax themselves to keep the city solvent. Most of them drive expensive cars like Audis, BMWs, Land Rovers, Range Rovers, Porsches, and Teslas. (Please note that I did not include Mercedes Benz in the above list. You seldom see a Mercedes with only one plate. Mercedes owners are old money, and old money people wouldn’t think of ignoring the law. They probably even tell the truth on their taxes.) Why do these scofflaws continue to thumb their noses at California Vehicle Code 5200(a) which states that “When two license plates are issued by the department for use upon a vehicle, they shall be attached to the vehicle for which they were issued, one in the front and the other in the rear.”? As Wiley sees it, there are two reasons: practicality and visual appeal. In the past few years, grilles on cars have grown so large (and ugly, IMHO) that there really isn’t much space below for a plate. Try attaching a license plate to a car where the grille takes up 90% of the front and let me know what happens. As for visual appeal, even Wiley will agree that a cool BMW or Porsche, with its sleek, tailored front styling, looks better without a plate disturbing its design. Installing a front plate would be like telling Zendaya (or Jennifer Anniston, if you are of Wiley’s generation) that she needs to do a better job on her makeup. But it is time for this lawlessness to come to an end. From a completely practical standpoint, the law makes sense. It makes it easier for ALPRs and police to recognize when something is out of whack. If CVC 5200(a) were enforced, any car without a front plate would be subject to a legal vehicle stop. I’m not saying that this would happen – PPD has enough on its hands that it wouldn’t and couldn’t. But it would give PPD the opportunity to conduct a vehicle stop if something didn’t seem right without being accused of racial or ethnic profiling. Now, Wiley is not saying that PPD should start enforcing the code tomorrow. Clearly, communication is key. PPD should choose a date several months in the future, publicize it widely, and begin putting notes on the windshields of parked cars without front plates informing the owners that they need to comply with the law. In other words, use a velvet glove. Finally, how do we deal with the outrage from Mr. Upstanding Citizen who gets his first ticket? Well, the ticket will be the “fix it” variety. So, MUC puts on the license plate that has been gathering dust in the garage, drives down to PPD HQ, and gets an officer to sign off on it. He then sends it in to the court and pays an administrative fee, probably $25. He and the missus may have to go without lattes from Starbucks for a day or two, but it will be an inexpensive life lesson. These days, it’s difficult to have a conversation with a Piedmont citizen without the subject of public safety coming up. As citizens, we need to do our part. We cannot rely on PPD, with its limited resources, to do everything. So, let’s make it easier for them to do their job and to protect us by putting those d**n front license plates on our cars. Note: Wiley’s wife drives a Tesla, which Wiley hates, but at least it has front and back license plates. Wiley Hoag is a Piedmont resident and the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs columnist.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 6, 2024 21 Features CONSUMER AFFAIRS Girl and her Dog Farm Michelle Docter and Rita show their harvest. Tucked behind a wooden fence in Albany lies a backyard you may not expect. Monarch butterflies and bees dance from sweet peas to broccoli. The classic Bay Area clay soil is worked with rich compost. Almost every inch of arable land holds an edible crop. This backyard isn’t just a backyard – it’s a farm and home to a small CSA program, Girl And Her Dog Farm, run by Michelle Docter and her dog Rita. This small Community Supported Agriculture feeds a handful of families every other week from spring to fall. Veggies, fruits, herbs, and fresh flower bouquets are all grown organically within the front and back yards and crafted into a produce box for delivery. Neighbors stop by while we refresh garden beds to admire the zinnias or ask how to stop the deer from devouring everything. Though small in size, the farm is creating community around homegrown food. Whether it’s a next door neighbor or a CSA member, they not only know who grows this food, but they’re learning about the variety of carrots planted. They get to see our growing practices that take a carrot from seed to soil and to their plate. While we’d love to curate produce boxes for all our neighbors, our Bay Area backyard just won’t cut it. The limited space in the backyard kindled our garden consulting service, teaching others how to grow food in their own space. After apprenticing at the UC Santa Cruz Farm, I want to share the skills and knowledge I learned on a big scale farm to a small-scale backyard. Growing just a small kitchen garden to snip herbs for a family meal or sowing enough lettuce for a weekly salad is what we hope to inspire and help create for all our neighbors. To spark that inspiration in our favorite way, my sweet dog and I jump in front of the camera, creating helpful videos on Youtube and Instagram. We share tips and tricks in the garden from starting a compost bin to planting a bed of tomatoes. There’s almost always something to make our audience smile. I’m delighted to also be writing a monthly column for the Piedmont Post where I can share more in depth gardening advice. With spring right around the corner, it’s the perfect time to start that garden you’ve always dreamed of. Now is actually a great time to add compost to your desired planting space and sow seeds, like: peas, lettuce, arugula, spinach, carrots, and beets. If starting on your own feels too daunting, please reach out. I’m excited to be able to help neighbors grow their own backyard farms. In fact, every time I have conducted an informal visual survey at the corner of Oakland and Highland, I have found that about half of the cars that go by have no front plates. My power of analytical thinking has led me to deduce that if a car has both front and back plates, it is significantly more likely to be recognized by the ALPR. And being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Let me repeat that: Being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Who are these scofflaws (what a great word)? Most of them are otherwise law-abiding citizens of Piedmont, who generally stop at stop signs, support our great police department, and keep voting to tax themselves to keep the city solvent. Most of them drive expensive cars like Audis, BMWs, Land Rovers, Range Rovers, Porsches, and Teslas. (Please note that I did not include Mercedes Benz in the above list. You seldom see a Mercedes with only one plate. Mercedes owners are old money, and old money people wouldn’t think of ignoring the law. They probably even tell the truth on their taxes.) Why do these scofflaws continue to thumb their noses at California Vehicle Code 5200(a) which states that “When two license plates are issued by the department for use upon a vehicle, they shall be attached to the vehicle for which they were issued, one in the front and the other in the rear.”? As Wiley sees it, there are two reasons: practicality and visual appeal. In the past few years, grilles on cars have grown so large (and ugly, IMHO) that there really isn’t much space below for a plate. Try Let’s be “Up Front” on license plates attaching a license plate to a car where the grille takes up 90% of the front and let me know what happens. As for visual appeal, even Wiley will agree that a cool BMW or Porsche, with its sleek, tailored front styling, looks better without a plate disturbing its design. Installing a front plate would be like telling Zendaya (or Jennifer Anniston, if you are of Wiley’s generation) that she needs to do a better job on her makeup. But it is time for this lawlessness to come to an end. From a completely practical standpoint, the law makes sense. It makes it easier for ALPRs and police to recognize when something is out of whack. If CVC 5200(a) were enforced, any car without a front plate would be subject to a legal vehicle stop. I’m not saying that this would happen – PPD has enough on its hands that it wouldn’t and couldn’t. But it would give PPD the opportunity to conduct a vehicle stop if something didn’t seem right without being accused of racial or ethnic profiling. Now, Wiley is not saying that PPD should start enforcing the code tomorrow. Clearly, communication is key. PPD should choose a date several months in the future, publicize it widely, and begin putting notes on the windshields of parked cars without front plates informing the owners that they need to comply with the law. In other words, use a velvet glove. Finally, how do we deal with the outrage from Mr. Upstanding Citizen who gets his first ticket? Well, the ticket will be the “fix it” variety. So, MUC puts on the license plate that has been gathering dust in the garage, drives down to PPD HQ, and gets an officer to sign off on it. He then sends it in to the court and pays an administrative fee, probably $25. He and the missus may have to go without lattes from Starbucks for a day or two, but it will be an inexpensive life lesson. These days, it’s difficult to have a conversation with a Piedmont citizen without the subject of public safety coming up. As citizens, we need to do our part. We cannot rely on PPD, with its limited resources, to do everything. So, let’s make it easier for them to do their job and to protect us by putting those d**n front license plates on our cars. Note: Wiley’s wife drives a Tesla, which Wiley hates, but at least it has front and back license plates. Wiley Hoag is a Piedmont resident and the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs columnist. articles.text: It’s time to save the date for the third annual Piedmont Food Fest. The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival is returning to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 20 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. This volunteer event was created post-pandemic, three years ago as a way to build community through diverse food, drink. and music. It has evolved into a broader showcase of the Bay’s most distinctive cuisines, cultural performances, and community groups. It has also attracted over 3000 attendees and generated over $100,000 for local businesses. Attendees have appreciated the chance to spend the day connecting with each other amid a medley of flavors, sounds, and cultures – all gathered in one place. “Piedmont Food Fest was an absolute treat for the whole family – a not-to-miss community event centered around connection and diversity,” said Havens parent Katie Castles Shaffer. “We love the Piedmont Food Fest, Being able to spend an afternoon with friends and community and have our kids entertained with the kids zone makes this an event we’ll look forward to every year. We especially appreciate the organizers’ dedication to having diverse representation of food, vendors and entertainment.” added Piedmont resident Amanda Feldman. Piedmont Food Fest 3 will feature over 19 food vendors including Crazy Empanadas, Robert Dorsey Catering, La Santa Torta, Momolicious, Arthur Mac’s, Lahor Di Khushboo, The Chairman, and Oakland Bloom as well as beer & wine tasting from local favorites including Federation Brewing, Two Broads Ciderworks, and Deer Hill Vineyards. Main stage performances will include Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, O Hina’aro Tahitian Dance & Music, Beloved Little Circus, and the Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator. Junior food festers can look forward to an enhanced KidZone with both carnival and multicultural craft stations. Please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org to sign up for event updates as well as checking out Early Bird specials available through March. This event is free to attend and all are encouraged to invite friends and family to come for a memorable day in Piedmont.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Quick soda bread with whole wheat and walnuts St. Patrick’s Day is just around the corner and the American tradition of corned beef and cabbage will be making an appearance on our table. I look forward to this time of year when I begin seeing corned beef appearing at our markets. I’ve previously shared my colcannon recipe, my family’s favorite dish of the meal, and now I’m sharing a quick soda bread I also prepare. You can toast the walnuts for additional flavor, as well as the wheat germ (if adding), but often I skip the toasting step and the bread is very tasty. This dough is pretty forgiving so you can take it to a sweet direction by adding a bit of dried fruit, or in a savory direction with some freshly snipped herbs and a bit of grated or tiny cubed cheese. Quick Soda Bread with Whole Wheat and Walnuts Adapted from America’s Test Kitchen, March 2013 Makes a one-pound loaf (approximate weight depending upon add-ins) INGREDIENTS • 1-1/4 cup all-purpose flour • 1/2 cup whole-wheat flour • 2 tablespoons wheat germ, toasted, optional • 1 tablespoon granulated sugar • 3/4 teaspoon sea salt • 3/4 teaspoon baking soda • 1/2 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped • 7 fl. ounces, 7/8 cup, buttermilk, chilled and preferably whole fat • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly; plus an additional 1 tablespoon melted to brush over the baked loaf INSTRUCTIONS Adjust an oven rack to the lower-middle position. Preheat the oven to 400° F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper and set aside. Whisk the flours, wheat germ (if using), sugar, salt, baking soda and powder together. Stir in the walnuts. Add the two tablespoons of melted butter into the chilled buttermilk. The butter will clump a bit when added to the cold buttermilk, which is what you want. Stir to break up any large lumps. These lumps of butter will translate into small, small, airy pockets in the finished loaf. Stir with a spatula until the dough just barely comes together. There will be some pockets of unincorporated flour and the dough will be shaggy, not at all cohesive. Turn onto a lightly floured surface then knead and turn a few times until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork the dough. It will be sticky but manageable. Shape into about a 4-1/2 to 5-inch round, about 2-inches tall. Place on the parchment lined baking sheet. Slice a large cross, or plus sign (+), about 1/4-inch deep and coming to about an inch from the edges with a sharp knife. The slicing is important to guide the bread’s expansion whilst it bakes. Bake about 45–50 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean, or about 195° F on an instant-read thermometer. Rotate the pan around midway through the baking. Remove the bread from the oven and brush on the remaining one tablespoon of melted butter. Transfer the loaf to a wire rack to cool for at least 30 minutes before slicing. articles.text: Dear Jim: I have water in my basement, and I’m experiencing flooding for the first time ever. I work out of my basement, so I need a permanent solution. Even the crawlspace next to it is wet and mold is developing. What should I do? Why is this happening? Most older homes in our area have inadequate drainage systems, and many have no drainage at all. Clay piping systems which were used as foundation drains when the homes were built were laid in small sections and are all filled with dirt and no longer working. Most downspouts still drain onto the ground next to your home, causing settlement problems and allowing water A new French drain is below the adjacent basement elevation. Dual membranes at the foundation provide additional protection. Flooded basements and crawlspaces need drainage help. inside. Add in climate change and extreme water events and this is a recipe for disaster. Why is this so difficult to fix? Most drainage work is done by landscapers, handymen, laborers or General Contractors who don’t understand the complexity of proper drainage. They make fundamental errors in designing their drainage solutions which often make the problems worse. The number of actual experienced drainage contractors in our area can probably be counted on one hand. What is the solution? Proper drainage generally consists of French Drains to handle underground water and separate downspout and area drains to handle surface water, and these are used in combination along with membranes to protect your foundation. Water needs to end up in either a drain field on your property or at the street. Sump pumps are most often only an external solution tied into your drainage system to remove water when the new drains can’t slope downhill to their endpoint. The location and depth of these drains and attention to detail particularly with the membrane system are crucial to their success. The Top 3 Things to remember: 1. Interior sump pumps are not the answer. When placed in your basement or crawlspace they typically only remove water directly adjacent to them. 2. You may need to go deep. French drains must extend at least a foot below the area they are trying to protect. Drainage that is too shallow will often make your problem worse. 3. Don’t fall for interior drainage solutions for your basement. While they are cheaper, drains on the inside next to your basement walls can undermine your foundations and don’t protect them from deterioration. articles.text: Bob Wright, a pillar of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20, 2024 of a heart attack while on vacation in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany. He was 80, and quite literally “died with his boots on”, while heading up the mountain for the last ski run of the day. He left this world as he lived in it, full of life and tackling adventures head on. Born Robert Bruce Wright on January 22, 1943, he was the son of William Bruce Wright and Thelma Brown Wright of Topeka, Kansas. Despite losing his father at a very young age, Bob grew up in a loving family and enjoyed a happy childhood. He was very active in the local Episcopal Church, serving as an altar boy for many years. He attended Topeka High School, where he was well liked and admired by his peers. After graduating from high school, Bob left Kansas for California, where he attended the University of the Pacific in Stockton. It was there he met the love of his life, his future wife Judith Meadows (later Wright). The two of them started out as “just good friends”, but eventually realized that there was a lot more than friendship there. The first year of their relationship was one of long distance, as Bob had been accepted to a year-long study abroad program in Denmark. Their commitment to each other remained steadfast, and excited to start their lives together as a married couple, they were married on August 28, 1965. Early in his marriage, Bob felt the call to serve his country, and joined the Marine Corps, serving a tour in Vietnam in 1967. After the birth of their first child, he chose to leave active duty military service in 1969, and continue his commitment to the Marines as an officer in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. He served for over 20 years and reached the rank of Colonel before retiring with full military honors in 1992. In addition to his military service, Bob had a distinguished career as a telecommunications Sales Executive with Pac Bell/AT&T, the culmination of which was an overseas assignment as Vice President of International Sales for Southeast Asia. Upon retirement from AT&T and his return to the U.S. in 1998, Bob continued his life of service. He was active in the community, most especially in the Piedmont Community Church. His love Bob Wright, a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20 while skiing in Germany on vacation. for and devotion to God and his church family were an ever-present part of his life. He served on multiple church boards, as well as headed multiple committees, projects, and small groups within the fellowship. His acts of charity, assistance, leadership and mentorship touched the lives of thousands. Everyone who knew Bob knew of his insatiable sense of wanderlust. Bob and Judy travelled extensively, managing to visit dozens of countries on all seven continents. He was an avid hiker, fisherman, and of course, skier. He threw himself with enthusiasm into high-adventure activities like ziplining well into his 70s. He was particularly a fan of cruising, and visited many exotic locations via Viking Ocean, River, and Expedition ships. He was never happier than when traveling with friends and family and sharing adventures with them. Bob is survived by his wife Judith Wright, and children Lisa Wright and Mitchell Wright. He is preceded in death by his parents, William and Thelma, stepfather Lenel Shuck, and sister Patricia. Bob will always be remembered for his charitable heart and love of life. We will miss him every day. The memory of him will live on in the hearts of all those who loved him. Bob will be remembered at a Celebration of Life service on Saturday, March 23, at 11:00 a.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Memorial donations in his name may be made to a charity of choice.

After graduating from high school, Bob left Kansas for California, where he attended the University of the Pacific in Stockton. It was there he met the love of his life, his future wife Judith Meadows (later Wright). The two of them started out as “just good friends”, but eventually realized that there was a lot more than friendship there. The first year of their relationship was one of long distance, as Bob had been accepted to a year-long study abroad program in Denmark. Their commitment to each other remained steadfast, and excited to start their lives together as a married couple, they were married on August 28, 1965. Early in his marriage, Bob felt the call to serve his country, and joined the Marine Corps, serving a tour in Vietnam in 1967. After the birth of their first child, he chose to leave active duty military service in 1969, and continue his commitment to the Marines as an officer in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. He served for over 20 years and reached the rank of Colonel before retiring with full military honors in 1992. In addition to his military service, Bob had a distinguished career as a telecommunications Sales Executive with Pac Bell/AT&T, the culmination of which was an overseas assignment as Vice President of International Sales for Southeast Asia. Upon retirement from AT&T and his return to the U.S. in 1998, Bob continued his life of service. He was active in the community, most especially in the Piedmont Community Church. His love Bob Wright, a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20 while skiing in Germany on vacation. for and devotion to God and his church family were an ever-present part of his life. He served on multiple church boards, as well as headed multiple committees, projects, and small groups within the fellowship. His acts of charity, assistance, leadership and mentorship touched the lives of thousands. Everyone who knew Bob knew of his insatiable sense of wanderlust. Bob and Judy travelled extensively, managing to visit dozens of countries on all seven continents. He was an avid hiker, fisherman, and of course, skier. He threw himself with enthusiasm into high-adventure activities like ziplining well into his 70s. He was particularly a fan of cruising, and visited many exotic locations via Viking Ocean, River, and Expedition ships. He was never happier than when traveling with friends and family and sharing adventures with them. Bob is survived by his wife Judith Wright, and children Lisa Wright and Mitchell Wright. He is preceded in death by his parents, William and Thelma, stepfather Lenel Shuck, and sister Patricia. Bob will always be remembered for his charitable heart and love of life. We will miss him every day. The memory of him will live on in the hearts of all those who loved him.
